lead: San Jose homes face creek flooding, aging pipes and winter storms. DryBeacon helps owners from Willow Glen to Evergreen get water out and dry quickly.
risk: creek flooding, pipe leaks in mid-century homes and winter storms
why: Coyote Creek overflowed in February 2017 and flooded the Rock Springs, Olinder and Naglee Park areas. Thousands of people were evacuated, and many renters lost belongings. The Guadalupe River and other creeks can rise during long winter storms too.

About 60% of San Jose homes were built before 1980. Ranch homes from the 1950s and 1960s often have original copper or galvanized pipes and slab foundations, which makes slab leaks common. Hillside homes in Almaden Valley and the East Foothills deal with runoff and drainage in wet winters.
image_alt: Homes and yard covered by creek floodwater
image_caption: Coyote Creek's 2017 flood reached thousands of San Jose homes and apartments.
problems: Homes near Coyote Creek and the Guadalupe River
tips: Check Valley Water flood maps if you live near a creek.
Renters near creeks should consider NFIP contents coverage.
Have old copper lines inspected for pinhole leaks.
Keep yard drains clear before winter storms.
areas: Calls come from Downtown, Willow Glen, Almaden Valley, Rose Garden, Evergreen, Japantown, Cambrian and Berryessa, plus Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Milpitas, Campbell and Los Gatos.

faq.q: What happened in the 2017 Coyote Creek flood?
faq.a: After heavy winter rain, Anderson Reservoir spilled and Coyote Creek overflowed in February 2017. Neighborhoods near the creek flooded, and about 14,000 people were told to evacuate. It showed how fast creek flooding can hit San Jose.
